problems.memo_sentence: "The authors use QAOA with classically optimized angle parameters as the core quantum method, and then apply transfer learning by taking parameters optimized on small bin packing problem (BPP) instances and reusing them on larger instances of BPP and on other COPs. They evaluate this both on multiple gate-based devices (IonQ Harmony and Aria, Rigetti Aspen-M-3, IBM Brisbane) and on a D-Wave Advantage annealer, where QAOA parameters are mapped into custom annealing schedules by modifying the s(t) mapping and A(s), B(s) schedules since only those schedule points are user-controllable."
problems.source_evidence: "D-Wave Advantage allows modification of the annealing schedule by specifying a maximum of 12 points for the relation si = f(ti) between a normalized time and instantaneous real-time. This flexibility enables us to implement a custom schedule for A(s) or B(s)." ... "Note that we modify D-Wave Advantage A(s) and B(s) schedules separately because the device does not allow the modification of both of them at the same time."
problems.explanation: The memo correctly notes that the schedules are user-controllable, but it omits the important limitation that only one of A(s) or B(s) can be modified at a time, not both jointly. That caveat matters for how the cross-platform transfer is implemented.

problems.memo_sentence: "The authors use QAOA with classically optimized angle parameters as the core quantum method, and then apply transfer learning by taking parameters optimized on small bin packing problem (BPP) instances and reusing them on larger instances of BPP and on other COPs."
problems.source_evidence: "We employ a quantum annealing initialization of the QAOA parameters [19, 31]."
problems.explanation: The memo omits that the QAOA parameters are initialized using a quantum annealing initialization scheme. This is a methodological detail explicitly stated in the paper and not reflected in the memo.

problems.memo_sentence: "The study finds that BPP is the best source problem for transferable QAOA parameters, yielding the strongest performance when transferred across COPs and maintaining a mean probability of finding the optimal solution above a quadratic-speedup-over-random-guessing threshold up to 42 qubits with p=10, although MaxCut is the weakest target among the problems considered."
problems.source_evidence: "The best performance and scaling trend are given by the KP. This scaling is not necessarily related to the TL capabilities because self-optimization shows a similar performance up to the size tested. The improvement could be related to the KP energy structure."
problems.explanation: The memo highlights BPP as the best transferable source, but it omits the paper's caveat that the best scaling trend in the larger-instance study is actually observed for KP and may not reflect transferability. This is a meaningful limitation on the interpretation of the scaling results.

problems.memo_sentence: "The authors primarily benchmark performance in terms of probability of finding the ground state relative to random guessing, using a quadratic-speedup-over-random-guessing line as a reference, and report that their transferred QAOA parameters maintain success probabilities above that threshold across the studied sizes."
problems.source_evidence: "Note that the probability(∗x) is preferred here instead of the approximation ratio r as it has been shown that r can be a misleading metric in constrained problems [39]."
problems.explanation: The memo describes the benchmark but does not mention why the authors prefer probability of success over approximation ratio. The paper explicitly states that approximation ratio can be misleading for constrained problems, which is an important limitation of alternative metrics.
